description_record.title: Supreme Court Agrees to Hear Challenge to Mandatory Immigrant Detention
description_record.description_short: Supreme Court agrees to hear the administration’s challenge to a ruling against mandatory detention without bond for certain immigrants.
description_record.description_medium: On October 1, the Supreme Court granted the federal government’s petition in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, agreeing to review a Second Circuit ruling against mandatory detention without bond for certain noncitizens already in the United States. The grant places the dispute on the Court’s new-term docket; it does not decide whether the policy is lawful. The case concerns a Brazilian national.
description_record.description_long: On October 1, 2026, the Supreme Court granted the government’s petition for review in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, docket 26-104. The case challenges a Second Circuit decision that rejected the administration’s use of an immigration statute to require detention without bond for people who had entered the United States unlawfully and were already living here. Reuters reported that the administration appealed after appellate courts ruled against the policy; the Court’s docket records the grant. The policy had been set out in Department of Homeland Security guidance in July 2025 and applies during removal proceedings, which can last months or years. The grant means the justices will consider the dispute in the new term. It is a procedural decision to hear the case, not a merits ruling, a nationwide injunction, or approval of mandatory detention. The underlying legal question remains open. The proceeding concerns the named petitioner’s case; it does not resolve every detention case covered by the administration’s guidance.

description_record.title: Judge Reinstates Roger Rogoff as U.S. Attorney for Western Washington
description_record.description_short: A federal judge reinstates Roger Rogoff and bars the administration from replacing him before a Senate-confirmed successor.
description_record.description_medium: On October 1, U.S. District Judge Stanley Bastian granted Roger Rogoff’s request for a preliminary injunction and ordered that he be reinstated as U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington. The order bars federal officials from treating another person as the district’s U.S. attorney while Rogoff holds the office, pending a Senate-confirmed replacement. It is preliminary relief in Rogoff’s lawsuit, not a final judgment.
description_record.description_long: Roger Rogoff was sworn in as U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington after a district court appointment in July 2026, then was removed by the administration less than an hour later. Rogoff challenged that removal. On October 1, 2026, U.S. District Judge Stanley Bastian granted his motion for a preliminary injunction after a hearing. The court’s order reinstated Rogoff and barred federal defendants from treating another person as the district’s U.S. attorney or obstructing Rogoff’s ability to perform the office’s duties. The dispute concerns the limits on presidential and Justice Department authority when a district court has appointed an interim U.S. attorney and the Senate has not confirmed a successor. It was an interim ruling while the case proceeds; it did not resolve all disputes about appointments in other districts or establish that every administration appointment was unlawful. The administration indicated it would seek appellate relief. This is the dated order restoring Rogoff, separate from prior litigation over appointment strategies and his July removal.

description_record.title: Florida Judge Dismisses Chelsea Cox’s Federal Voting Case
description_record.description_short: A Florida judge dismisses Chelsea Cox’s case, holding the federal noncitizen-voting statute unconstitutional as applied to her.
description_record.description_medium: On October 1, U.S. District Judge David Leibowitz dismissed the federal voting case against Chelsea Cox, a Jamaican national charged over her 2020 ballot. His 31-page opinion held 18 U.S.C. § 611 unconstitutional as applied to Cox and dismissed the information. The ruling resolves her federal case; it is not binding on other judges, and state prosecutors could still consider state-law charges.
description_record.description_long: On October 1, 2026, U.S. District Judge David Leibowitz dismissed the federal information against Chelsea Michelle Ann Cox in the Southern District of Florida. Cox, a Jamaican national and Florida resident, had been charged with a misdemeanor for allegedly voting in the 2020 election. The judge’s 31-page opinion concluded that Congress lacked authority to apply 18 U.S.C. § 611 to Cox’s alleged conduct and dismissed the federal prosecution. The holding was framed as an as-applied ruling in this case, not a nationwide injunction against the statute; the opinion recognized that different constitutional questions could arise for elections in the District of Columbia. CBS reported that state prosecutors could still pursue a state-law case. This is the court’s disposition of one prosecution during the administration’s broader attention to alleged noncitizen voting. It does not establish that Cox’s vote changed an election outcome or decide other prosecutions. The government may appeal, and the sources reviewed do not establish whether any appeal had been filed by October 3.

description_record.title: Judge Temporarily Blocks Publication of New University Foreign-Donor Identities
description_record.description_short: A judge temporarily bars the Education Department from publishing previously undisclosed foreign-donor identities reported under Higher Education Act § 117.
description_record.description_medium: On October 1, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order in the Association of American Universities’ case against the Education Department. The order bars publication of previously undisclosed identifying information about foreign donors and contract counterparties reported by member institutions under Section 117. It lasts 28 days unless extended and does not cover 92 foreign entities the department had already published in July.
description_record.description_long: The Association of American Universities sought emergency relief after the Education Department announced plans to publish identifying information that colleges had reported under Section 117 of the Higher Education Act. Following an October 1, 2026 hearing, U.S. District Judge Tanya S. Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order barring the department and other defendants from publishing previously undisclosed identities of foreign donors and contract counterparties reported by AAU member institutions. The order also bars other steps to carry out the department’s publication decision. AAU’s case challenges the department’s decision and revised reporting approach; the organization says the department had previously assured institutions that donor identities would remain confidential. The court found AAU likely to succeed on its arbitrary-and-capricious claim at this preliminary stage, according to AAU’s case update. The restraint runs for 28 days unless extended and does not cover 92 foreign entities whose information had already been published on July 15. The order does not resolve the merits or establish that all Section 117 reports must remain confidential.

description_record.title: Judge Blocks Border-Barrier Construction in Texas’ Big Bend Sector
description_record.description_short: A judge bars border-barrier construction and ground disturbance in Big Bend until federal officials comply with applicable law.
description_record.description_medium: On October 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone granted a preliminary injunction in Friends of the Ruidosa Church v. Mullin. The order bars DHS and CBP from building border barriers or related infrastructure, or disturbing ground, in the Big Bend sector until they comply with applicable laws. It applies despite the administration’s waivers and remains in effect until further court order.
description_record.description_long: On October 2, 2026, Judge Kathleen Cardone granted plaintiffs’ motion for a preliminary injunction in Friends of the Ruidosa Church v. Mullin, a Western District of Texas case. The signed order immediately barred DHS, Customs and Border Protection, and covered federal defendants from constructing border barriers or related infrastructure, or undertaking construction or ground-disturbing work, in the Big Bend sector unless and until they comply with applicable laws. The order states that compliance is required notwithstanding the administration’s Big Bend waivers, including the West Waiver and National Park Waiver. The court issued the injunction after considering testimony, exhibits, legal authorities, and arguments. The order is preliminary and remains in force until the court orders otherwise; it does not resolve all claims or permanently prohibit construction. Separate border-wall litigation and waivers involve other sectors and different orders, so this entry is limited to Cardone’s October 2 ruling and its geographic scope.
